content: The Pidgeon process is a method for producing magnesium metal through silicothermic reduction. The energy required for practical production is approximately 35-40 MWh per ton of magnesium, which is comparable to molten salt electrolytic methods but significantly higher than the theoretical minimum of 7 MWh per ton. Chemistry The fundamental chemical reaction involves silicon reacting with magnesium oxide to produce silica and magnesium. Although this reaction is thermodynamically unfavorable according to Ellingham diagrams, it can proceed by applying Le Chatelier's principle. This is achieved by continuously supplying heat and removing magnesium vapor, one of the reaction products, through distillation. Magnesium has a low boiling point of 1090°C at atmospheric pressure, and this boiling point is even lower under vacuum conditions. Vacuum is preferred as it allows the reaction to occur at lower temperatures. The most commonly used and cost-effective form of silicon in this process is ferrosilicon alloy. The iron in the alloy does not participate in the reaction and acts as a spectator. The magnesium oxide used as the raw material can be obtained through various methods. For example, magnesium chloride from seawater or lake water can be hydrolyzed to magnesium hydroxide, which is then calcined to magnesium oxide by removing water. Alternatively, mined magnesite (MgCO₃) can be calcined to magnesium oxide by removing carbon dioxide. The most widely used raw material is dolomite, a mixed calcium-magnesium carbonate (Ca, Mg)CO₃. During the reaction, calcium oxide scavenges the silica formed, releasing heat and consuming one of the products, which helps drive the equilibrium forward. The Pidgeon process is a batch process. Finely powdered calcined dolomite and ferrosilicon are mixed, briquetted, and loaded into retorts made of nickel-chrome-steel alloy. The reaction zone of the retort is heated using gas, coal, or electricity in a furnace, while the condensing section, equipped with removable baffles, extends from the furnace and is water-cooled. The distillation process produces high-purity magnesium crowns, which are then remelted and cast into ingots. Carbothermic Reduction Challenges Using carbon as a reducing agent instead of silicon is not feasible in this process. Silicon dioxide is a solid, while carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide are gaseous. These gaseous products would follow the magnesium vapor and reverse the reaction, leading to the reformation of the initial reactants. Although a process using carbon and shock-freezing of vapors to prevent the reverse reaction is theoretically possible, it is not economically viable for industrial applications. At temperatures where magnesium is still liquid or solid (600-700°C) and carbon oxides are gaseous, the thermodynamic counterforces make the reactions impractical, even if carbon monoxide were purged with argon and the argon recycled. The equilibrium can theoretically be driven forward, but the reaction rates are so slow that it would take decades to achieve detectable results, making it industrially unfeasible. At lower temperatures, the reaction energetics dominate, and silicon outperforms carbon as a reducing agent. This is because silicon dioxide has a much larger heat of formation compared to carbon oxides, as shown in Ellingham diagrams. Historical Background The Pidgeon process was invented in the early 1940s by Dr. Lloyd Montgomery Pidgeon of the Canadian National Research Council (NRC). The first plant was built in 1941 and operated by Dominion Magnesium in Haley, Ontario, Canada. This plant operated for 63 years, most recently under Timminco Metals. Over the last decade, the Pidgeon process has become the dominant method for global magnesium production. China is now the leading supplier of magnesium metal, relying almost exclusively on this method. World Market Issues Before the mid-1990s, the global magnesium market was dominated by electrolytic processes, with the United States as the primary supplier. For over 80 years, Dow Chemical operated a 65 kton/year plant near Freeport, Texas, using seawater-extracted magnesium chloride electrolysis. This plant was the main magnesium supplier until its closure in 1998. As of 2005, the only U.S. producer is US Magnesium in Utah, a company that emerged from the now-defunct Magcorp. Severe anti-dumping tariffs are being imposed on Chinese imports. In 2005, the U.S. produced about 45 ktons out of a global 615 kton/year capacity (7%), compared to 140 ktons out of 311 kton/year (45%) in 1995. In contrast, China now produces 400 ktons out of 615 kton/year (65%), compared to 12 ktons out of 311 kton/year (4%) in 1995. The price of magnesium metal dropped from $2300/ton in 1995 to $1300/ton by 2001 but climbed back above $2300/ton by 2004 due to increased costs for ferrosilicon, energy, and transportation, as well as the anticipation of severe anti-dumping duties worldwide. The energy efficiency of thermal processes like the Pidgeon method is comparable to electrolytic methods, both requiring approximately 35-40 MWh per ton. The Pidgeon process is technologically simpler, and due to the distillation and vapor deposition conditions, it easily produces a high-purity product. Historically, besides the U.S., major magnesium producers included Norsk Hydro of Norway/Canada, the former Soviet Union countries, Brazil, and France, all of which had access to cheap and abundant hydroelectric or nuclear power. Recently, Israel has entered the global magnesium market, while the Australian company Magnesium International is planning a 100 kton/year smelter in Sokhna, Egypt, using the Dow electrolytic process.
